archetype.name: Bubble Team (power-play driven)
archetype.definition: A sub-.500 club in a soft Pacific whose elite power play and hot finishing keep it in games that its 5-on-5 play and last-ranked goaltending keep giving away.

report.headline: The league's best power play is papering over the league's worst goaltending.
report.take:
Anaheim at 11-12-1 is a team pulling in two directions at once. The offense ranks 6th in goals a game at 3.63, but that output leans heavily on a power play converting at 34.2%, first in the league and far above the 22.5% league average. Behind it sits a defense ranked 29th in goals allowed at 3.83 a game, and the reason for that is mostly in net. The goaltending grade is an F. Team save percentage is .858, 32nd of 32, against a league mark of .891, and Goalies GSAx is -10.7, 31st.

The goaltending collapse is not mainly a product of shot volume. Anaheim allows 25.9 shots on goal a game, 11th-fewest, and its CF % sits at a dead-average 50%. Both goalies are underwater even after GSAx adjusts for shot quality: Lukas Dostal at .857 and -5.8, Ville Husso at .854 and -3.3, ranked 58th and 65th of 72 on the goalie tab. The 5-on-5 picture is still not clean, though. The xGF % of 45.4% ranks 27th, so the chances Anaheim gives up are better than the ones it creates even when it holds the puck as much as its opponent. That is a real step back from last season's 51.9%.

The numbers hide a pair of offsetting distortions. The scoring is inflated: a power play that converted 18.6% last year and 11.8% the year before will not stay at 34%, and an 11.3% team shooting rate against a 9.8% league norm will also drift down. The goals against are deflated past what this roster should allow, because no NHL tandem stays at .858 forever. One more point on the goalies: last year's group finished at -12.8 GSAx with the same 29th-ranked defense, and the team still reached 92 points and won six playoff games. Bad goaltending here is a pattern, not a blip. Pts vs Goal Diff at -2.3 says the record is, if anything, a little behind the differential.

The trajectory is choppy. A 5-8 October gave way to a run of four straight wins to open November, then a 1-4 slide over the last five, with 4.4 goals allowed a game. The pace is 79 points, which would usually miss the playoffs. But the Pacific is thin, with Seattle in third at 10-9-1, so Anaheim's season hinges on whether the goaltending recovers before the power play cools.

strengths.title: Best power play in hockey
strengths.body: At 34.2%, Anaheim's power play leads the league and runs well clear of the 22.5% average. It is the single biggest reason a 27th-ranked xGF % team ranks 6th in scoring. It will regress, since the last two seasons ran at 18.6% and 11.8%, but even a cooled version is a weapon against bad penalty kills.

strengths.title: Finishing above the league
strengths.body: Skaters are shooting 11.3% in all situations, 9th in the league and well above the 9.8% norm. That turns modest chance creation into goals, and November's 4.0 goals a game shows it at full strength. Some of this is power-play driven and some is variance, so expect it to slide toward average rather than hold.

strengths.title: Shot volume against is manageable
strengths.body: Anaheim allows only 25.9 shots on goal a game, 11th-fewest, and holds an even 50% CF %. The volume of pressure is not what is sinking it. That matters, because it means ordinary goaltending would fix much of the goals-against problem.

concerns.title: Last-ranked goaltending, again
concerns.body: A .858 team save percentage ranks 32nd, and Goalies GSAx of -10.7 ranks 31st, with neither Dostal nor Husso holding up. Last season's group finished at -12.8 GSAx, so this is a recurring weakness rather than a slump. Some recovery toward average is likely, but the history argues against counting on a full fix.

concerns.title: Losing the chance battle at 5-on-5
concerns.body: The xGF % of 45.4% ranks 27th, down from 51.9% last season. The puck is shared evenly, but the dangerous looks tilt the other way. Opposing wingers have feasted, outscoring their own averages against Anaheim by more than all but a few defenses allow, and wingers take a well-above-league share of the points against. This one is structural and will not regress on its own.

concerns.title: Recent slide is defensive
concerns.body: The last five games went 1-4 with 4.4 goals allowed a game, including eight against in St. Louis. Scoring also dipped to 3.2 a game over that stretch, so the cushion the offense usually provides disappeared. If the power play cools before the goaltending steadies, this is what a normal week looks like.

trend.note: A 5-8 October turned into a four-game win run to open November, then a 1-4 skid over the last five. Results swing on whether the power play and finishing outrun the goaltending on a given night.

weekAhead.headline: Four division games against weak penalty kills, and a goaltending test.
weekAhead.body:
All four games are against Pacific rivals sitting at or near Anaheim in the standings, and all three opponents rank lower on the site. The week opens at Seattle, then brings San Jose to Anaheim, then a home-and-home with Los Angeles on consecutive days. The common thread is the matchup Anaheim most wants: the league's best power play meets three below-average penalty kills. Seattle's is 32nd at 60.7%, Los Angeles 29th at 69.1% and San Jose 21st at 73.9%.

The catch is that none of these games is safe with a .858 save percentage behind the skaters. San Jose arrives with Goalies GSAx of 7.8 and an A+ forward grade. Los Angeles is better than its 7-12-2 record, with an xGF % of 50.4% and a Pts vs Goal Diff of -3.4 that points to bad luck. A winning week is very available here, but given the last five games it is not guaranteed.

keyMatchups.title: Power play vs. Seattle's broken kill
keyMatchups.body: Seattle kills only 60.7% of penalties, last in the league, while Anaheim converts 34.2%, first. Seattle also posts the league's worst CF % at 42%, so Anaheim should have the puck and draw calls. This is the best chance all week to bank a win.

keyMatchups.title: San Jose's hot goalies, leaky wingers
keyMatchups.body: San Jose's goalies sit at 7.8 GSAx, and its 2.4 Pts vs Goal Diff shows a team winning more than its play suggests. The Sharks also allow 30.4 shots a game, 31st, and rank last at holding wingers to their averages. Anaheim's wingers should get volume; the question is whether it beats a goalie group outperforming expectations.

keyMatchups.title: Kings home-and-home tightens the game
keyMatchups.body: Los Angeles holds opposing forwards well below their averages, 7th overall and 1st against centers, and its xGF % beats Anaheim's. The Kings' 69.1% PK is the opening, so special teams likely decide these two games. Their -7.4 GSAx means neither crease is likely to steal one.

weekAhead.watch: Whether Dostal or Husso can post even league-average save numbers for a week. Against these penalty kills the offense will show up; the goaltending decides whether it adds up to points.

restOfSeason.body:
Expect the two extremes to pull back toward the middle. The power play will not finish anywhere near 34%, and the above-average shooting will drift down, so the 3.63 goals a game should ease. On the other side, a .858 save percentage is about as low as a tandem gets, and some recovery is likely even if this crease stays below average as it did last year. The 5-on-5 chance deficit, with an xGF % of 45.4%, is the part that worries me, because it is the real talent signal and it fell sharply from last season.

The net picture is a team that plays like a fringe club and sits on a pace for 79 points. Its saving grace is the division: the Pacific behind Edmonton and Vegas is mediocre, so a playoff spot is reachable with something in the mid-80s. I project roughly 78 to 88 points. The ceiling depends almost entirely on the goaltending moving from catastrophic to merely below average.
swingFactors: Dostal's save percentage recovering toward league average
How fast the power play cools from 34%
Pacific third place staying within reach

confidence.note: 24 games is a real sample, but the save percentage and power-play extremes are volatile and both are likely to move.
